articles.title: Three Hundred and Fifty Thousand Indian New Zealanders Are About to Meet a Prime Minister Who Took Forty Years to Arrive
articles.excerpt: Modi's July 10 visit to New Zealand will be the first by an Indian PM in four decades. For a diaspora that now makes up six per cent of the country and generates $350 million in GDP, it is less a diplomatic event than a recognition long overdue.
articles.image_caption: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi — his upcoming visit to New Zealand will be the first by an Indian PM in 40 years
articles.nri_angle: New Zealand's Indian community — now 350,000 strong and six per cent of the population — awaits the first visit by an Indian PM in 40 years, navigating between diplomatic warmth and tightening immigration rules.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Received a Record $145 Billion From Its Diaspora. For the First Time, America Sent the Most.
articles.excerpt: Inward remittances hit $144.79 billion in FY26, up from $124.55 billion the year before. The bigger story is where the money is coming from — and what the shift says about who the Indian diaspora has become.
articles.image_caption: The Reserve Bank of India headquarters in Mumbai — India received a record 44.79 billion in diaspora remittances in FY26
articles.nri_angle: America is now the single largest source of remittances to India, overtaking the Gulf — a data-driven confirmation of the diaspora's shift from blue-collar Gulf workers to white-collar US professionals.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: She Left Kerala at Six. Now Nithya Raman Wants to Run America's Second-Largest City.
articles.excerpt: The urban planner turned Los Angeles city councillor has secured a spot in the November mayoral runoff against incumbent Karen Bass, making her the first Indian-born candidate to seriously contend for the office.
articles.image_caption: Nithya Raman, Los Angeles city councillor for the 4th district, in her 2022 official portrait
articles.nri_angle: Raman's journey from a Malayali immigrant family in Louisiana to the doorstep of LA's top job encapsulates the expanding arc of Indian American political ambition — no longer limited to state legislatures and Congress, but now reaching for executive power in the country's biggest cities.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: One Dollar a Day, Millions of Children: The Diaspora Gala Betting That Indian Education Is the Best Investment on Earth
articles.excerpt: The Vidyabharati Foundation of America will gather tech leaders, philanthropists, and MIT's Ramesh Raskar in Boston this Sunday to fundraise for one of India's largest school networks — at a per-pupil cost that shames most Western aid budgets.
articles.image_caption: MIT professor Ramesh Raskar, keynote speaker at the Vidyabharati Foundation of America's 2026 annual gala in Boston
articles.nri_angle: The gala embodies a maturing pattern in NRI philanthropy — moving from writing cheques for hometown temples to funding scalable, institution-grade educational infrastructure in India, with the same venture-capital rigour that built careers in Silicon Valley and Route 128.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Twelve Dance Schools Took Carnegie Hall's Biggest Stage. Every Performer Was Born in America.
articles.excerpt: The All-Indian Dance Festival 2026 brought Kuchipudi, Bharatanatyam, and Odissi to the Stern Auditorium — performed by suburban kids trained in strip-mall studios, and backed by a $10 million bet that Indian classical arts belong in America's most storied concert hall.
articles.image_caption: The Isaac Stern Auditorium at Carnegie Hall, New York City. (Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0)
articles.nri_angle: American-born Indian youth performing ancestral classical dance forms at Carnegie Hall represents the ultimate test of whether these traditions can survive transplantation — and thrive — far from their origins.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Real Estate Just Had Its Best Half-Year in Six Years. Here Is What NRIs Need to Know.
articles.excerpt: Institutional investment hit $4.5 billion, Mumbai registrations reached a 14-year high, and office leasing broke all records. For the diaspora eyeing property back home, the numbers are loud — but the fine print matters.
articles.image_caption: Mumbai skyline along Marine Drive, the financial capital driving India's property boom
articles.nri_angle: NRIs account for roughly 19% of Indian property purchases. With the rupee above 90/USD, repo rates at 5.25%, and the new digital-only eOCI card reducing bureaucratic friction, 2026 is a particularly compelling window for diaspora real estate investment — but FEMA repatriation rules and market shifts demand careful planning.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Vancouver's Indian Summer Festival Returns With 90 Artists, Free Programming, and a Theme That Asks the Diaspora to Listen
articles.excerpt: The 16th edition of Canada's largest South Asian arts festival opens July 9 with 'Ragas for a Ruptured World' — a provocation aimed squarely at a diaspora navigating belonging in unsettled times.
articles.nri_angle: Indian Summer Festival is one of North America's premier South Asian cultural events, rooted in Vancouver's large Punjabi and South Asian diaspora. Its free programming in Surrey's Punjabi Market and partnership with Indo-Canadian artists make it a direct expression of diaspora cultural identity and cross-generational connection.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America's Fastest-Growing Diaspora Is Getting Old. The Safety Net Barely Exists.
articles.excerpt: In Queens, an AI-powered food pantry is feeding 1,500 South Asian seniors a year. In Irvine, a new wellness centre serves elders who speak no English. Across the country, a crisis is building that the community has only begun to name.
articles.image_caption: America's Indian diaspora is aging rapidly, and community support systems for elderly immigrants remain scarce (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The aging of the first large wave of Indian immigrants to the US and the growing phenomenon of 'parent visas' — elderly parents brought over to help with grandchildren — has created a uniquely diaspora elder care crisis. Language barriers, cultural isolation, unfamiliarity with American social services, and the shame associated with admitting family cannot cope are all distinctly NRI dimensions of the problem.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Central Bank Is Paying NRIs Up to Seven Per Cent to Park Their Dollars at Home. Here Is the Catch.
articles.excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India has opened a rare deposit window that eliminates currency risk for overseas Indians — but the fine print includes a three-year lock-in and a September deadline.
articles.image_caption: The Reserve Bank of India headquarters in Mumbai's Fort district
articles.nri_angle: Directly impacts NRI savings strategy — overseas Indians can now earn 5.5-7% on dollar deposits in India with zero currency risk, a significant premium over US savings accounts. The scheme specifically targets Gulf and US-based NRIs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Eight Michelin Stars, a Whole Foods Aisle, and a Cancer Survivor's Dream: Indian Food's American Moment Is Here
articles.excerpt: From a Sethi siblings' sauce line in every Whole Foods to a 7,500-square-foot Charlotte clubhouse run by a Hyderabad-trained chef, Indian cuisine is making its most ambitious play yet for the American mainstream.
articles.image_caption: Indian cuisine has arrived on America's fine-dining stage — from Michelin stars to Whole Foods aisles (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin chefs and entrepreneurs are leading the mainstreaming of Indian cuisine in America — from Michelin-starred restaurants to grocery store aisles. The movement reflects how the diaspora is reshaping American food culture from within, not just opening ethnic restaurants but building national consumer brands.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Twenty-Six Thousand Indian Australians Signed Up for a Stadium Reception. Then Came the Death Threat.
articles.excerpt: The 'Melbourne Meets Modi' reception at Marvel Stadium on July 9 has become the largest Indian diaspora gathering ever planned in Australia — and one of the most contested.
articles.image_caption: Marvel Stadium in Melbourne's Docklands, where up to 26,000 Indian Australians are expected on July 9
articles.nri_angle: Australia's million-strong Indian-born community navigates competing emotions — rockstar excitement and rising hostility — as it prepares to host Modi in a country still debating how much room to make for its largest overseas-born population.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Melbourne Spent $1.2 Million to Build Australia's First 'Little India.' Not Everyone Is Celebrating.
articles.excerpt: Backed by the city's biggest cultural budget in years, the Docklands precinct would join Chinatown and Koreatown as an officially recognised cultural hub — but not without a fight.
articles.image_caption: Melbourne's Docklands waterfront, the planned site of Australia's first officially recognised Little India precinct
articles.nri_angle: For the quarter-million Indian-born Melburnians who have long lacked a geographic cultural home, the precinct signals institutional acceptance — and reveals the tensions that come with it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
